mcq.explanation: `pwd` (print working directory) prints the absolute path of the directory you are currently in.
mcq.distractors: `ls` lists contents, `cd` changes directory and `mv` moves or renames files.

mcq.explanation: `ls -a` lists all entries, including hidden dotfiles such as `.bashrc` and the `.` and `..` entries.
mcq.distractors: `pwd`, `rm` and `mkdir` do not list files; `rm -a` and `mkdir -a` are not valid options.

mcq.explanation: `chmod` changes file permissions (read, write, execute for user, group and others), e.g. `chmod 755 script.sh`.
mcq.distractors: Ownership is changed with `chown`/`chgrp`, the hostname with `hostnamectl`, and interfaces with `ip`.

mcq.explanation: `grep` searches text in files for lines matching a pattern, e.g. `grep -rn ERROR logs/`.
mcq.distractors: `pwd` prints the directory, `touch` creates files or updates timestamps, and `mv` moves files.

mcq.explanation: `cat` displays a file's contents (it concatenates files to standard output).
mcq.distractors: `kill` signals processes, `rmdir` removes empty directories and `mkdir` creates directories.

mcq.explanation: The pipe `|` passes one command's output (stdout) to another command's input, e.g. `ps aux | grep nginx`.
mcq.distractors: Redirecting to a file is `>` or `>>`; the pipe has nothing to do with root privileges or deleting files.

mcq.explanation: `ps` shows running processes, e.g. `ps aux` for all processes; `top`/`htop` show them live.
mcq.distractors: `cp` copies, `ls` lists files and `mkdir` creates directories.

mcq.explanation: `cd` changes the current directory, e.g. `cd /var/log` or `cd ..`.
mcq.distractors: `echo` prints text, `pwd` only shows where you are, and `cat` prints file contents.

mcq.explanation: `sudo` lets a permitted user run commands with elevated privileges (as root by default), as configured in `/etc/sudoers`.
mcq.distractors: Pulling images is `docker pull`, symlinks come from `ln -s`, and DNS records from `dig`/`nslookup`.

mcq.explanation: `df -h` shows disk space usage by filesystem (size, used, available, mount point) in human-readable units.
mcq.distractors: `du` reports space used by files/directories, `free -m` shows memory and `uname -a` shows kernel info.

labs.modelAnswer:
# create the structure
mkdir -p ~/project/{app,logs,config}
cd ~/project

# sample files
echo 'print("hello")' > app/main.py
echo 'ERROR disk full' > logs/app.log
echo 'INFO started' >> logs/app.log
echo 'port=8080' > config/app.conf
touch app/notes.txt

# list
ls -la
ls -R

# copy and move
cp config/app.conf config/app.conf.bak
mv app/notes.txt logs/notes.txt

# search
grep -rn 'ERROR' logs/
find . -name '*.conf'

# delete
rm config/app.conf.bak
rm logs/notes.txt
ls -R
labs.explanation: Tests everyday file management: building a directory tree, creating files, and using ls, cp, mv, grep/find and rm. When verifying, check that `mkdir -p` (or brace expansion) builds all three subdirectories, and that each operation is followed by an `ls` or similar so the result is visible. Be careful with `rm -r`: always confirm the path first.

checks.label: Adds the user to the group (usermod -aG / gpasswd -a)

labs.modelAnswer:
sudo groupadd devops
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash examuser
sudo passwd examuser        # set a password interactively
sudo usermod -aG devops examuser
id examuser                  # shows devops in the group list

# project directory owned by the group
sudo mkdir -p /opt/project
sudo chown -R examuser:devops /opt/project
sudo chmod -R 2770 /opt/project   # rwx for owner and group, nothing for others; setgid keeps new files in group devops
ls -ld /opt/project
# drwxrws--- 2 examuser devops 4096 ... /opt/project
labs.explanation: Tests user and group administration plus ownership and permissions. Key point: `usermod -aG` must include `-a` (append) or the user is removed from other supplementary groups. Verify with `id examuser` and `ls -ld`; the setgid bit (2 in 2770) makes new files inherit the devops group, which is useful for shared team directories. Group membership only applies to new login sessions.

checks.label: Simulates the failure (stop / kill / bad config)
Checks port, process or config (ss / ps / nginx -t)

labs.modelAnswer:
# 1. Check the service
systemctl status nginx          # Active: active (running) / failed, plus last log lines
systemctl is-active nginx

# 2. Simulate a problem: break the config and restart
sudo cp /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.bak
echo 'this is not valid;' | sudo tee -a /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
sudo systemctl restart nginx    # fails

# 3. Diagnose
systemctl status nginx          # shows 'failed'
journalctl -u nginx -n 50 --no-pager   # recent logs for this unit
journalctl -u nginx --since '10 min ago'
sudo nginx -t                   # config test points at the bad line
sudo tail -n 20 /var/log/nginx/error.log
ss -tlnp | grep ':80'           # is anything listening on port 80?
ps aux | grep [n]ginx

# 4. Fix and verify
sudo cp /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.bak /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl restart nginx
systemctl status nginx
curl -I http://localhost
labs.explanation: Tests a systematic service troubleshooting workflow with systemd: status, logs via `journalctl -u <unit>`, then narrowing the cause (config test, listening ports, process list) before fixing and re-verifying. A good answer documents each command and what its output told you, and ends by proving the service is healthy again.
